description: Ruby's classroom: ecosystem lore, agent culture, on-chain history, general knowledge.

questions.subject: general-knowledge
questions.prompt: What does HTTP stand for?

options.B: High-Test Token Passing

questions.explanation: Tim Berners-Lee, 1989. The 'S' came later.

questions.subject: ai-literacy
questions.prompt: In an AI app, what does it usually mean when a model can use a tool?

options.B: It can call an external function or API

questions.explanation: Tool use lets the model ask software to do bounded work, like search, fetch data, or update a record.

questions.subject: general-knowledge
questions.prompt: What year did Bitcoin's whitepaper appear?
questions.explanation: October 31, 2008. Satoshi Nakamoto shared the paper on a cryptography mailing list.

questions.subject: ai-literacy
questions.prompt: In a classroom chat with several AI helpers, what does shared context help everyone do?

options.B: Stay aligned on the same room, task, and participants

questions.explanation: Shared context keeps the helpers oriented to the same people, lesson, and current goal.

questions.subject: general-knowledge
questions.prompt: Which Solana program type holds executable code?

options.B: Program

questions.explanation: Programs are read-only Account-resident binaries; user state lives in separate Accounts.

questions.subject: ai-literacy
questions.prompt: Why do AI apps often store embeddings in a vector database?

options.B: To search items by semantic similarity
options.D: To remove the need for evaluation

questions.explanation: Embeddings turn text or media into vectors; vector search finds nearby meanings rather than exact keyword matches.

questions.subject: general-knowledge
questions.prompt: In a B-tree of order m, what's the maximum number of children per node?

options.B: m

questions.explanation: Order m means up to m children, m-1 keys per non-leaf node.

questions.subject: ai-literacy
questions.prompt: When several AI agents collaborate in one classroom, which information should be visible to all helpers in that room?

options.B: The room's lesson state and recent turns

questions.explanation: Room-level lesson state helps agents coordinate without exposing private secrets.

questions.subject: general-knowledge
questions.prompt: Which sorting algorithm has a worst-case O(n log n) AND is in-place?

options.B: Mergesort

questions.explanation: Heapsort is in-place with O(n log n) worst case. Quicksort is O(n²) worst, mergesort needs O(n) extra space.

questions.subject: agent-culture
questions.prompt: What is the safest default for an AI agent before it takes an irreversible action?

options.B: Retry until it works

questions.explanation: Irreversible actions need a human confirmation step unless the user has already granted a narrow, explicit permission.

questions.subject: general-knowledge
questions.prompt: Which protocol does HTTPS layer over TCP?

options.B: SSH

questions.explanation: Transport Layer Security; SSL was its predecessor.

questions.subject: general-knowledge
questions.prompt: What does 'API' stand for?

options.B: Application Programming Interface

questions.explanation: Application Programming Interface. Coined in the 1960s for subroutine-call contracts.

questions.subject: agent-culture
questions.prompt: In MCP (Model Context Protocol), what does a 'tool' return to the model?

options.B: Structured content blocks

questions.explanation: MCP tools return content blocks — text, images, resources — that the model includes in context.

questions.subject: general-knowledge
questions.prompt: What's the time complexity of a hash table lookup in the average case?

options.B: O(log n)

questions.explanation: Constant on average; O(n) worst case with adversarial collisions.

questions.subject: ai-literacy
questions.prompt: What does an evaluation set help reveal about an AI feature?

options.A: Whether the feature works on examples held back from prompt tuning
options.B: Whether the model has the largest context window
options.C: Whether the UI color palette is accessible
options.D: Whether API latency is always zero

questions.explanation: A held-out evaluation set catches regressions and overfitting: the system has to work on cases it was not tuned against.

questions.subject: ai-literacy
questions.prompt: Why is an idempotency key useful when an agent retries a purchase-like tool call?

options.A: It makes the model more creative
options.B: It lets the server recognize the retry as the same operation
options.C: It hides the request from logs

questions.explanation: Idempotency keys prevent duplicate side effects when a request is retried after a timeout or network failure.

questions.subject: agent-culture
questions.prompt: In an agent workflow, why should durable state be written before acknowledging a completed external action?

options.A: So the UI can use a bigger font
options.B: So recovery after a crash does not forget the action happened

questions.explanation: If the process crashes after the external action but before persistence, the system can lose track of real-world side effects.

questions.subject: ai-literacy
questions.prompt: Before an AI app posts from your account, what should it do?

options.B: Post silently

questions.explanation: Actions that affect an account need clear consent before they run.

questions.subject: general-knowledge
questions.prompt: What does DNS stand for?

options.B: Digital Network Service

questions.explanation: DNS translates domain names to IP addresses. It's the phonebook of the internet.

questions.subject: general-knowledge
questions.prompt: What is a 'pull request' in software development?

options.B: A proposal to merge changes into a codebase

questions.explanation: Pull requests are how teams review and integrate code changes before they land.

questions.subject: general-knowledge
questions.prompt: Which of these is a NoSQL database?

options.B: MySQL

questions.explanation: MongoDB stores documents rather than rows. PostgreSQL, MySQL, and SQLite are relational.

questions.subject: general-knowledge
questions.prompt: What does a CDN (Content Delivery Network) primarily improve?

options.B: Static asset load times by serving from nearby edges

questions.explanation: CDNs cache content at edge locations so users hit a nearby server instead of the origin.

questions.subject: general-knowledge
questions.prompt: What is the purpose of a load balancer?

options.B: To distribute incoming requests across multiple servers

questions.explanation: Load balancers prevent any single server from being overwhelmed and enable horizontal scaling.

questions.subject: general-knowledge
questions.prompt: In Git, what does 'git rebase' do differently from 'git merge'?

options.B: Rebase replays commits onto a new base, producing a linear history
options.C: Rebase only works on the main branch
options.D: Rebase is the same as merge but faster

questions.explanation: Rebase rewrites commit history to be linear. Merge preserves the branch topology.

questions.subject: general-knowledge
questions.prompt: What does 'containerization' (e.g., Docker) provide?

options.B: Isolated environments that package an app with its dependencies

questions.explanation: Containers bundle everything an app needs to run, making deployments consistent across machines.

questions.subject: general-knowledge
questions.prompt: What is the CAP theorem in distributed systems?

options.A: Consistency, Availability, Partition tolerance — you can only guarantee two
options.B: Compute, Analyze, Publish — the three stages of data processing

questions.explanation: Eric Brewer's CAP theorem: a distributed data store can only provide two of the three guarantees simultaneously.

questions.subject: general-knowledge
questions.prompt: What is a Bloom filter used for?

options.B: Probabilistic set membership testing with space efficiency

questions.explanation: A Bloom filter can tell you 'definitely not in the set' or 'maybe in the set' using very little memory.

questions.subject: general-knowledge
questions.prompt: What does 'eventual consistency' mean in distributed databases?

options.B: All replicas will converge to the same value given enough time without new writes
options.D: Only the primary node has correct data

questions.explanation: In eventually consistent systems, replicas may temporarily diverge but will converge once writes stop propagating.

questions.subject: general-knowledge
questions.prompt: What problem does the Two Generals' Problem illustrate?

options.B: The impossibility of guaranteed agreement over an unreliable channel

questions.explanation: It's a thought experiment showing that two parties cannot be certain they've agreed if their communication channel can fail.

questions.subject: ai-literacy
questions.prompt: What does 'LLM' stand for?

options.B: Large Language Model

questions.explanation: Large Language Models are the foundation of modern AI chat, trained on vast text corpora.

questions.subject: ai-literacy
questions.prompt: What is a 'hallucination' in AI?

options.A: When the model runs faster than expected
options.B: When the model generates plausible-sounding but incorrect information
options.C: When the model refuses to answer
options.D: When the model uses too much memory

questions.explanation: Hallucinations are confident fabrications. The model doesn't know it's wrong.

questions.subject: ai-literacy
questions.prompt: What is the purpose of 'temperature' in LLM sampling?

options.A: To control the model's physical heat output
options.B: To control randomness — lower = more deterministic, higher = more creative

questions.explanation: Temperature = 0 gives nearly deterministic output. Higher values increase variety at the cost of coherence.

questions.subject: ai-literacy
questions.prompt: What does RAG stand for in AI applications?

options.B: Retrieval-Augmented Generation

questions.explanation: RAG fetches relevant documents and feeds them into the prompt so the model can reference real data instead of relying on training memory.

questions.subject: ai-literacy
questions.prompt: Why is 'prompt injection' a security concern?

options.B: A user or third party can override system instructions by embedding commands in input
options.D: It disables the model's safety filter

questions.explanation: Prompt injection tricks the model into ignoring its system prompt. It's the AI equivalent of SQL injection.

questions.subject: ai-literacy
questions.prompt: What is a 'token' in the context of LLMs?

options.B: A unit of text the model processes — roughly a word or subword

questions.explanation: Models break text into tokens before processing. Pricing and context windows are measured in tokens.

questions.subject: ai-literacy
questions.prompt: What does 'chain-of-thought prompting' encourage the model to do?

options.B: Show intermediate reasoning steps before giving a final answer

questions.explanation: Asking the model to 'think step by step' dramatically improves accuracy on reasoning tasks.

questions.subject: ai-literacy
questions.prompt: What is the 'alignment tax' in AI safety research?

options.B: The potential performance trade-off when making a model safer or more aligned with human values
options.C: A regulatory fee for AI companies

questions.explanation: Making models safer can reduce raw capability. The alignment tax is the gap between helpful-only and helpful-and-harmless.

questions.subject: ai-literacy
questions.prompt: What is a key limitation of transformer attention mechanisms at very long context lengths?

options.B: Quadratic memory and compute cost relative to sequence length
options.C: They can only process English text
options.D: They require special hardware for any input

questions.explanation: Standard self-attention is O(n²) in sequence length, which is why long-context models need tricks like sparse or ring attention.

questions.subject: ai-literacy
questions.prompt: In RLHF (Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback), what are human evaluators typically asked to do?

options.B: Rank or compare model outputs to train a reward model

questions.explanation: Humans compare pairs of model outputs. A reward model learns to predict human preferences, then fine-tunes the base model.

questions.subject: ai-literacy
questions.prompt: What does it mean when a model has a 'system prompt' vs. a 'user prompt'?

options.B: The system prompt sets persistent behavior rules; the user prompt is the specific query
options.C: The system prompt is always hidden from users
options.D: User prompts override system prompts completely

questions.explanation: System prompts are the persistent instruction layer — 'you are a helpful tutor.' User prompts are the conversation turns.

questions.subject: agent-culture
questions.prompt: What is an 'AI agent' typically defined as?

options.B: Software that perceives its environment and takes actions to achieve goals

questions.explanation: Agents sense, decide, and act. The key distinction from a chatbot is autonomous action-taking.

questions.subject: agent-culture
questions.prompt: What does it mean for an agent to be 'stateless'?

options.B: Each request is independent — it doesn't remember previous interactions

questions.explanation: Stateless agents treat every request as new. Stateful agents carry context across turns.

questions.subject: agent-culture
questions.prompt: What is a 'multi-agent system'?

options.A: A single model running on multiple GPUs
options.B: Multiple AI agents working together, each with specialized roles or tools
options.D: A model trained on multiple languages

questions.explanation: Multi-agent systems decompose complex tasks across specialized agents that coordinate through messages or shared state.

questions.subject: agent-culture
questions.prompt: What is the 'tool-use divide' in agent design?

options.A: Whether to use open-source or proprietary tools
options.B: Deciding which capabilities live as model reasoning vs. which get delegated to external tools
options.C: Splitting work between CPU and GPU

questions.explanation: Every agent design decision is: does the model reason about this, or does it call a function? The boundary matters.

questions.subject: agent-culture
questions.prompt: Why do agent frameworks often include a 'reflection' or 'self-critique' step?

options.B: To let the agent review its own output and improve it before sending

questions.explanation: Self-critique loops let the agent catch errors, refine reasoning, or decide whether to retry with different tools.

questions.subject: agent-culture
questions.prompt: What is a 'guardrail' in agent development?

options.B: A safety constraint that prevents the agent from taking dangerous or undesired actions

questions.explanation: Guardrails are the rules, filters, and checks that constrain what an agent can actually do — the fence around the playground.

questions.subject: agent-culture
questions.prompt: What is the 'paperclip maximizer' thought experiment meant to illustrate?

options.B: How a misaligned optimization goal can lead to catastrophic outcomes even from a seemingly harmless objective

questions.explanation: Nick Bostrom's thought experiment: an AI told to maximize paperclip production could convert all matter into paperclips. The goal is technically met.

questions.subject: agent-culture
questions.prompt: What does 'instrumental convergence' mean in AI alignment?

options.A: That all AI models converge on the same architecture
options.B: That many different final goals imply the same intermediate sub-goals like self-preservation and resource acquisition
options.D: That instruments are needed for alignment

questions.explanation: Whether your goal is to make paperclips or cure cancer, you'll likely need to stay alive and acquire resources first. Those are convergent instrumental goals.

questions.subject: agent-culture
questions.prompt: Why is 'sandboxing' important when letting an agent execute code?

options.A: It makes the code run faster
options.B: It isolates execution so the agent can't damage the host system or access sensitive data

questions.explanation: Sandboxing limits what executed code can touch — filesystem, network, processes. Without it, agent-written code runs with the host's privileges.

questions.subject: agent-culture
questions.prompt: What distinguishes 'tool-use' from 'agentic behavior'?

options.B: Tool-use is calling a function when asked; agentic behavior is the model deciding when and which tool to call as part of pursuing a goal

questions.explanation: Tool-use is mechanistic. Agency is the loop: observe, decide, act, observe again. The model drives the cycle.

questions.subject: general-knowledge
questions.prompt: What does SQL stand for?

options.B: Structured Query Language

questions.explanation: SQL is the lingua franca of relational databases. Declarative, set-based, nearly 50 years old and still running the world.

questions.subject: general-knowledge
questions.prompt: What is the purpose of a firewall?

options.B: To filter incoming and outgoing network traffic based on security rules

questions.explanation: A firewall is the bouncer at the network door. It decides what packets get in and what gets dropped.

questions.subject: general-knowledge
questions.prompt: What does 'open source' mean?

options.A: Software that is free of bugs
options.B: Software whose source code is publicly available and can be inspected, modified, and distributed
options.C: Software that runs on any operating system

questions.explanation: Open source is about access to the code. Linux, Firefox, Python — built in public, maintained by communities.

questions.subject: general-knowledge
questions.prompt: What is a race condition in concurrent programming?

options.A: When two programs compete for speed
options.B: When the behavior of a program depends on the timing or ordering of uncontrollable events
options.C: When a program runs faster than expected

questions.explanation: Two threads reaching for the same variable at the same time. The outcome depends on who gets there first. These are famously hard to reproduce and debug.

questions.subject: general-knowledge
questions.prompt: What problem does OAuth solve?

options.B: Delegated authorization — letting a service act on your behalf without sharing your password

questions.explanation: 'Sign in with Google' without giving Google your password to the third party. OAuth is a delegation protocol, not an authentication protocol — though it's often used as one.

questions.subject: general-knowledge
questions.prompt: What is the difference between TCP and UDP?

options.A: TCP is faster; UDP is more reliable
options.B: TCP guarantees ordered, error-checked delivery; UDP is connectionless and faster but doesn't guarantee delivery
options.D: TCP is for video; UDP is for text

questions.explanation: TCP: three-way handshake, acknowledgments, retransmission. UDP: fire and forget. Streaming and gaming prefer UDP; web browsing needs TCP.

questions.subject: general-knowledge
questions.prompt: What is a Merkle tree used for in distributed systems?

options.B: Efficiently verifying data integrity — each leaf is a hash, and parent nodes hash their children

questions.explanation: Bitcoin, Git, Certificate Transparency — all use Merkle trees. You can verify a piece of data belongs in a large dataset without downloading the whole thing.

questions.subject: general-knowledge
questions.prompt: What is the Byzantine Generals' Problem?

options.B: The challenge of reaching consensus in a distributed system when some participants may be malicious or faulty

questions.explanation: Some generals may be traitors sending conflicting messages. How do the loyal ones agree on a plan? This is the foundational problem that blockchain consensus mechanisms attempt to solve.

questions.subject: general-knowledge
questions.prompt: What does 'idempotent' mean in the context of API design?

options.A: The API always returns the same data
options.B: Making the same request multiple times produces the same side effect as making it once

questions.explanation: PUT is idempotent. POST is not. If a network hiccup causes a retry, idempotent operations are safe to repeat. This is why payment APIs use idempotency keys.

questions.subject: ai-literacy
questions.prompt: What is 'training data' in machine learning?

options.A: Data used to test the model
options.B: The dataset used to teach a model patterns before it's deployed

questions.explanation: Training data is the textbook. The model learns statistical patterns from it. Garbage in, garbage out is the first law of ML.

questions.subject: ai-literacy
questions.prompt: What does GPT stand for?

options.B: Generative Pre-trained Transformer

questions.explanation: Pre-trained on vast corpora, then fine-tuned. The Transformer architecture (2017) made modern LLMs possible.

questions.subject: ai-literacy
questions.prompt: What is 'fine-tuning'?

options.A: Making small adjustments to a model's physical hardware
options.B: Further training a pre-trained model on a specific dataset to specialize its behavior
options.D: Translating the model to another language

questions.explanation: You take GPT-4, train it further on your legal documents or medical texts, and it becomes better at your domain. The base capabilities transfer; the specialization is learned.

questions.subject: ai-literacy
questions.prompt: What is a 'context window'?

options.A: The browser window the AI runs in
options.B: The maximum amount of text (measured in tokens) the model can consider at once
options.D: The number of users who can use the model simultaneously

questions.explanation: Everything you've ever said to the model that it can still 'see' fits in the context window. Early GPT models had 2K tokens. Modern ones have 128K+.

questions.subject: ai-literacy
questions.prompt: What is 'emergent behavior' in large language models?

options.B: Capabilities that appear at scale that weren't explicitly trained for — like chain-of-thought reasoning or theory of mind
options.D: The model learning a new language on its own

questions.explanation: Smaller models can't do certain tasks at all. Scale up 10x and suddenly they can. Nobody taught them — the capability emerged from the combination of scale, data, and architecture.

questions.subject: ai-literacy
questions.prompt: What is the difference between 'supervised' and 'unsupervised' learning?

options.A: Supervised uses labeled data (input → expected output); unsupervised finds patterns in unlabeled data
options.B: Supervised requires human supervision during inference

questions.explanation: Supervised: here are 10,000 pictures labeled 'cat' or 'dog', learn to classify. Unsupervised: here are 10,000 pictures, find clusters. Most LLM pre-training is self-supervised — a clever variant of unsupervised.

questions.subject: ai-literacy
questions.prompt: What is a 'latent space' in machine learning?

options.B: A compressed, abstract representation where similar concepts are close together — the model's internal 'map' of meaning

questions.explanation: In embedding space, 'king' - 'man' + 'woman' ≈ 'queen'. The model learns a geometry of concepts. Latent space is where the thinking actually happens.

questions.subject: ai-literacy
questions.prompt: What problem does 'knowledge cutoff' refer to?

options.A: The model refusing to answer certain questions
options.B: The model's training data stops at a specific date — it knows nothing about events after that point
options.C: The maximum length of model responses

questions.explanation: GPT-4 was trained on data up to a certain month. Ask about something that happened after and it's guessing or hallucinating. RAG and web search are partial workarounds.

questions.subject: agent-culture
questions.prompt: What makes an AI 'agentic' rather than just 'generative'?

options.A: It generates images instead of text
options.B: It can take actions, use tools, and pursue goals across multiple steps without being prompted at each step

questions.explanation: A chatbot answers when asked. An agent decides what to do next. The difference is autonomy over the action loop.

questions.subject: agent-culture
questions.prompt: What is 'chain of thought' in the context of tool-using agents?

options.A: A fixed sequence of tool calls
options.B: The agent thinks through what tool to call and why, possibly interleaving reasoning and action
options.D: A UI pattern for chat interfaces

questions.explanation: ReAct pattern: Thought → Action → Observation → Thought. The agent reasons about what it knows, decides what to do, observes the result, and reasons again.

questions.subject: agent-culture
questions.prompt: What is a 'human-in-the-loop' workflow?

options.A: A human sitting at a desk near the server
options.B: The agent pauses at critical decision points and asks for human approval before proceeding
options.D: The model training on human conversations

questions.explanation: Before an agent sends an email, makes a purchase, or posts publicly, it asks. The loop is: agent proposes, human approves, agent executes. Trust but verify.

questions.subject: agent-culture
questions.prompt: What is 'specification gaming' in AI systems?

options.B: The agent finds a way to achieve the literal reward or objective while violating the spirit of what was intended
options.C: The agent writes its own specifications

questions.explanation: A robot told to 'minimize falling' learns to lie down and never move. A cleaning robot told to 'hide messes' learns to turn off its cameras. The spec was technically met.

questions.subject: agent-culture
questions.prompt: What is the difference between 'orchestration' and 'chaining' in agent workflows?

options.B: Chaining is a linear sequence of calls; orchestration is dynamic — the agent decides the next step based on previous results

questions.explanation: Chain: A → B → C, always. Orchestrate: A, then if result looks like X do B, otherwise do D. Orchestration is the agent making decisions mid-flight.

questions.subject: agent-culture
questions.prompt: What is a 'code execution sandbox' for AI agents?

options.B: An isolated environment where agent-generated code runs with restricted permissions — no network, no filesystem access, resource limits

questions.explanation: The agent writes and runs code, but in a jail. It can compute, but it can't exfiltrate data, install malware, or fork-bomb the host. Every agent that runs code needs one.

questions.subject: agent-culture
questions.prompt: What is the 'tool selection' problem in multi-tool agents?

options.A: Deciding which programming language to use
options.B: Given many available tools, the agent must decide which one is appropriate for the current sub-goal — and the wrong choice wastes time or produces garbage

questions.explanation: An agent with 50 tools is not 50x more capable — it's 50x more likely to pick the wrong one. Tool curation and clear descriptions matter more than tool count.

questions.subject: general-knowledge
questions.prompt: What is the difference between a process and a thread?

options.B: A process has its own memory space; threads share memory within a process

questions.explanation: Processes are isolated. Threads are lightweight workers within a process that share the same address space. The trade-off is isolation vs. overhead.

questions.subject: general-knowledge
questions.prompt: What does 'ACID' stand for in database transactions?

options.B: Access, Control, Integrity, Deletion

questions.explanation: The four guarantees that make transactions safe: all-or-nothing (Atomicity), valid state transitions (Consistency), invisible intermediate states (Isolation), permanent writes (Durability).

questions.subject: general-knowledge
questions.prompt: What is the purpose of a reverse proxy?

options.B: To sit in front of backend servers, handling client requests and routing them — often adding SSL termination, caching, and load balancing

questions.explanation: Nginx, HAProxy, Envoy. The reverse proxy is the front door: clients talk to it, it talks to your servers. It hides your architecture and handles cross-cutting concerns.

questions.subject: ai-literacy
questions.prompt: What is a 'vector embedding'?

options.B: A numerical representation of text (or other data) where semantic similarity maps to geometric proximity

questions.explanation: 'Cat' and 'kitten' have vectors close together. 'Cat' and 'democracy' are far apart. Embeddings are how models do semantic search, clustering, and retrieval.

questions.subject: ai-literacy
questions.prompt: Why do LLMs sometimes repeat themselves or get stuck in loops?

options.B: The model's probability distribution collapses — it keeps selecting tokens that lead back to the same state
options.D: The training data had too many repetitions

questions.explanation: Repetition loops are a known failure mode. Once the model starts repeating, the repetition itself becomes the most likely next token. Temperature and repetition penalties help break the cycle.

questions.subject: ai-literacy
questions.prompt: What is 'catastrophic forgetting' in neural networks?

options.B: When fine-tuning on new data, the model rapidly loses performance on previously learned tasks
options.C: The model forgets its own name

questions.explanation: You fine-tune your model on legal documents and suddenly it can't write poetry anymore. The new knowledge overwrites the old. Continual learning is an open research problem.

questions.subject: agent-culture
questions.prompt: What is a 'prompt' in the context of AI?

options.B: The input text given to a model to instruct or query it

questions.explanation: The prompt is the interface. It's simultaneously instruction, context, and question. Prompt engineering is learning to speak the model's language.

questions.subject: agent-culture
questions.prompt: What does 'few-shot prompting' mean?

options.A: Asking the model very few questions
options.B: Providing a few examples in the prompt to show the model what kind of output you want
options.C: Training the model on a few examples

questions.explanation: Show the model 2-3 examples of the task, then ask it to do the same. The pattern recognition happens in the context window, not in training.

questions.subject: agent-culture
questions.prompt: What is 'constitutional AI'?

options.A: An AI that follows the constitution
options.B: An approach where the model is trained to follow a set of principles (a 'constitution') and self-critiques its outputs against those principles
options.C: An AI system for legal work
options.D: An AI trained only on constitutional law

questions.explanation: Anthropic's approach: give the model rules, have it critique its own outputs against them, and use those critiques for RL training. The constitution replaces some of the human feedback.

questions.subject: agent-culture
questions.prompt: What is the 'outer alignment' vs. 'inner alignment' distinction?

options.A: Alignment of external vs. internal APIs
options.B: Outer alignment: does the training objective match what we want? Inner alignment: does the model that emerges from training actually internalize that objective?

questions.explanation: You can specify the right objective (outer alignment) but the optimization process might produce a model pursuing something else entirely (inner misalignment). The specification is not the specification.

questions.subject: general-knowledge
questions.prompt: What is a 'bug' in software?

options.A: A literal insect in the computer
options.B: An error, flaw, or unintended behavior in a computer program

questions.explanation: The term allegedly originated from a moth found in a Harvard Mark II relay in 1947. Grace Hopper taped it into the logbook. The metaphor stuck.

questions.subject: general-knowledge
questions.prompt: What is the difference between 'encryption' and 'hashing'?

options.B: Encryption is reversible with a key; hashing is one-way and produces a fixed-size output
options.C: Hashing is reversible; encryption is not

questions.explanation: Encrypt to hide data (reversible). Hash to verify integrity (one-way). You can decrypt ciphertext; you can't 'dehash' a hash. Passwords should be hashed, never encrypted.

questions.subject: general-knowledge
questions.prompt: What does 'CI/CD' stand for?

options.B: Continuous Integration / Continuous Delivery (or Deployment)

questions.explanation: CI: merge code frequently, run automated tests. CD: automatically deploy passing builds. The pipeline that turns commits into shipped software.

questions.subject: ai-literacy
questions.prompt: What is 'prompt engineering'?

options.B: The practice of designing effective prompts to get desired outputs from language models

questions.explanation: It's part art, part science. Knowing how to structure instructions, provide examples, and constrain outputs. The prompt is the programming language of LLMs.

questions.subject: ai-literacy
questions.prompt: What is a 'foundation model'?

options.A: A model only for construction work
options.B: A large model trained on broad data that can be adapted to many downstream tasks
options.D: A model that runs on basic hardware

questions.explanation: GPT-4, Claude, Gemini — these are foundation models. They're not built for one task; they're built to be adaptable to thousands. The foundation enables the house.

questions.subject: ai-literacy
questions.prompt: What is 'reinforcement learning from human feedback' (RLHF) trying to solve?

options.B: Aligning model behavior with human preferences when the 'correct' answer is subjective or hard to specify

questions.explanation: Some tasks have no single right answer. 'Write a helpful email' — what's helpful? RLHF trains a reward model on human preference comparisons, then fine-tunes the LLM to maximize that reward.

questions.subject: agent-culture
questions.prompt: What is 'prompt chaining'?

options.B: Using the output of one LLM call as input to the next, building a pipeline of transformations
options.C: A type of neural network architecture

questions.explanation: Step 1: summarize this article. Step 2: extract key claims from the summary. Step 3: fact-check each claim. Each step is a separate LLM call, each informed by the previous.

questions.subject: agent-culture
questions.prompt: What is 'recursive self-improvement' in AI?

options.A: The model learning from its own outputs during inference
options.B: An AI system that can improve its own code or architecture, potentially triggering a rapid capability increase
options.C: The model retraining on user feedback

questions.explanation: This is the core of many AI risk arguments. If an AI can make itself smarter, and the smarter version can make itself even smarter... the curve gets steep fast. This remains theoretical but is taken seriously.

questions.subject: general-knowledge
questions.prompt: What is 'technical debt'?

options.B: The implied cost of future rework caused by choosing an easy solution now instead of a better approach that would take longer

questions.explanation: Ward Cunningham's metaphor. Every shortcut, every 'we'll fix it later,' every skipped test compounds. You pay interest in slower development, more bugs, and harder changes.

questions.subject: general-knowledge
questions.prompt: What is the difference between 'vertical' and 'horizontal' scaling?

options.A: Vertical is up-down; horizontal is left-right
options.B: Vertical: adding more power to existing servers. Horizontal: adding more servers
options.D: Vertical scaling requires more code changes

questions.explanation: Scale up (bigger machine) vs. scale out (more machines). Vertical hits physical limits. Horizontal requires distributed systems thinking but can scale effectively without bound.

questions.subject: ai-literacy
questions.prompt: What is 'model distillation'?

options.A: Converting a model to a different format
options.B: Training a smaller 'student' model to mimic the behavior of a larger 'teacher' model
options.D: Splitting a model across multiple GPUs

questions.explanation: The large model generates outputs; the small model learns to reproduce them. The result is a much smaller model that captures much of the teacher's capability. Distillation is how you get GPT-4-level quality into a phone-sized model.

questions.subject: agent-culture
questions.prompt: What is the simplest definition of an 'API'?

options.B: A defined way for two pieces of software to communicate — a contract of inputs and outputs

questions.explanation: Application Programming Interface. It's the menu: you tell the kitchen what you want (input), they bring you food (output). You don't need to know how the kitchen works.

questions.subject: general-knowledge
questions.prompt: What does 'URL' stand for?

options.B: Uniform Resource Locator

questions.explanation: Tim Berners-Lee, 1994. The address bar. Protocol + domain + path. The web's fundamental navigation primitive.

questions.subject: general-knowledge
questions.prompt: What is 'zero-downtime deployment'?

options.A: Deploying when nobody is using the app
options.B: Updating a running service without any period where requests fail or users see errors

questions.explanation: Blue-green, rolling, canary — patterns for swapping out running software while traffic keeps flowing. The users should never notice a deploy happened.

questions.subject: ai-literacy
questions.prompt: What does it mean for a model to 'overfit'?

options.A: The model is too large to deploy
options.B: The model memorizes training data patterns so specifically that it fails to generalize to new data
options.D: The model uses too many parameters

questions.explanation: Perfect scores on the practice test, fails the real exam. Overfitting is learning the noise, not the signal. Regularization, dropout, and more diverse training data help.

questions.subject: agent-culture
questions.prompt: What is 'goal misgeneralization'?

options.A: Setting goals that are too broad
options.B: An AI system learns the correct behavior during training but pursues a different (often related) goal when deployed in a new environment

questions.explanation: The agent was trained to navigate mazes and always took the shortest path. Deploy it in a new maze and it takes the shortest path — even if that path goes through a wall. The capability generalized; the goal didn't.
